pos: n. (the central Spanish kingdom of Isabella and Cisneros, which founded the Spanish Inquisition in 1478 and produced the Complutensian Polyglot)
etymology: From Spanish Castilla, from Latin castellum, a castle, for the frontier castles of the Duero.
biblical_def: Castile is the kingdom of the central Spanish plateau whose union with Aragon through Isabella and Ferdinand made Spain. Two decisions of Isabella's reign govern this dictionary's account of her kingdom. In 1478 she obtained from Sixtus the Fourth a bull creating an Inquisition under royal rather than papal control, the first of its kind, aimed at conversos suspected of secretly keeping Jewish practice; in 1492 the Jews who would not be baptised were expelled. And in 1499 her confessor Francisco Jimenez de Cisneros, archbishop of Toledo, founded the university of Alcala and commissioned the Complutensian Polyglot, the first printed Bible setting Hebrew, Greek, Aramaic and Latin in parallel columns, finished in 1517 and the finest work of biblical scholarship then produced anywhere. The dictionary records both from the same hand. Castile gave the church one of its great critical Bibles and gave Europe the model of a confessional police state, and it did so through the same reforming churchman. Scholarship is not holiness, and a man may serve the text in print while hunting the people who read it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a polyglot as a book of several languages; an inquisition as a court for the examination of heretics; expulsion as the act of driving out; a convert as one turned from one faith to another; and scholarship as learning or erudition.
webster_full: POLYGLOT, a. Having or containing many languages; as a polyglot bible or lexicon. n. A book containing many languages.
INQUISITION, n. In some catholic countries, a court or tribunal established for the examination and punishment of heretics.
EXPULSION, n. The act of driving out or away; a driving away by violence; the state of being driven out.
CONVERT, n. A person who is converted from one opinion or practice to another; particularly, a person who renounces error and embraces the truth.
SCHOLARSHIP, n. Learning; attainments in science or literature; literary education.
scriptures: Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Rom 10:2
For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.

Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
corruption_summary: Central Spanish kingdom of Isabella and Cisneros, founder of the Spanish Inquisition in 1478 and producer of the Complutensian Polyglot of 1517.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is learned religion without a converted heart, and Castile puts the two side by side so clearly that no commentary is required. Cisneros paid for Hebrew and Greek types out of his own revenues, and he also organised the forced baptism of the Muslims of Granada in defiance of the treaty of surrender. A church that produces both has a problem the printing press cannot touch. Isaiah's word to a nation of correct observance fits it exactly: “this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me” (Isa 29:13).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Faith is seated where no tribunal can reach, which is why compelled profession is not profession: “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom 10:10). Paul's diagnosis of zealous Israel is the dictionary's verdict on Castilian religion, that it had fervour aimed at the wrong thing, “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). And the Polyglot the kingdom produced contains the instrument that would have corrected it, the living text itself, “For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12).

pos: n. (the eastern Spanish crown of Ferdinand, whose medieval inquisition was absorbed into the Castilian tribunal after the killing of Pedro de Arbues in 1485)
etymology: From Spanish Aragón, from the river Aragón in the Pyrenean foothills.
biblical_def: The crown of Aragon was a federation rather than a kingdom: Aragon proper, Catalonia, Valencia, Majorca, and in the later Middle Ages Sardinia, Sicily and Naples, each with its own laws and assemblies which the king swore to keep. Ferdinand's marriage to Isabella in 1469 joined it to Castile. Aragon had possessed a papal inquisition since the thirteenth century, directed at the Albigenses and later at conversos, and when the new royal tribunal was extended there in 1484 it was resisted as a breach of Aragonese liberties; the inquisitor Pedro de Arbues was murdered in the cathedral of Saragossa in 1485, after which the resistance collapsed and the tribunal became permanent and feared. The dictionary records Aragon because it is the clearest sixteenth-century demonstration that constitutional liberties do not survive a religious emergency. The Aragonese had charters, courts and a standing right of protest, and they lost all of it in a single season to an argument about heresy. A free people may be talked out of its freedoms by being frightened.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a charter as a written instrument conferring privileges; a federation as a league; privilege as a particular benefit enjoyed; emergency as a pressing necessity; and tyranny as arbitrary exercise of power.
webster_full: CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract or privileges conferred.
FEDERATION, n. The act of uniting in a league; confederacy; a union of states by compact.
PRIVILEGE, n. A particular and peculiar benefit or advantage enjoyed by a person, company or society, beyond the common advantages of other citizens.
EMERGENCY, n. The rising of one thing out of another; a sudden or unexpected occasion; pressing necessity.
TYRANNY, n. Arbitrary or despotic exercise of power; the exercise of power over subjects with a rigor not authorized by law.
scriptures: The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
Luk 12:4
And I say unto you my friends, Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?
corruption_summary: Eastern Spanish crown whose constitutional resistance to the royal Inquisition collapsed after the murder of the inquisitor Pedro de Arbues at Saragossa in 1485.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is government by fright, and Aragon shows the mechanism in a single year. A people with real charters objected to a tribunal that ignored them; one inquisitor was killed; and thereafter opposition to the tribunal was itself treated as complicity in his death, so the charters lapsed in practice without ever being repealed. Solomon identifies the hinge, which is interior rather than legal: “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe” (Pro 29:25).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Christ addresses fear directly and limits what an enemy can actually do, telling his friends to “Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do” (Luk 12:4). The ground on which a subject refuses an unlawful command is apostolic and brief, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29), and the psalmist supplies the confidence that makes a man able to say it in a courtroom: “The LORD is on my side; I will not fear” (Psa 118:6). Liberties are kept by people who are not frightened, and the dictionary says plainly that no charter has ever substituted for that.

pos: n. (the Atlantic kingdom which forcibly baptised its Jews in 1497, received the Inquisition in 1536, and carried the Roman mission to Africa, India, Brazil and Japan)
etymology: From Latin Portus Cale, the harbour of Cale at the mouth of the Douro, the modern Oporto.
biblical_def: Portugal is the oldest fixed frontier in Europe and the first of the seaborne empires. In 1496 Manuel the First ordered the Jews expelled and then, unwilling to lose them, had the children seized and baptised in 1497 and declared the whole community Christian, creating an entire population of nominal converts with no instruction and every reason for concealment; the Lisbon massacre of 1506 killed thousands of them. The Inquisition was established in 1536 chiefly to police that population, and its tribunals at Lisbon, Evora, Coimbra and Goa ran until 1821. At the same time Portuguese ships carried the Roman mission further than any Western church had gone: Africa, Brazil, India, Malacca, China and Japan, with Francis Xavier sailing from Lisbon in 1541. The dictionary records both halves as one story. The same crown that manufactured false Christians at home financed the greatest missionary expansion since the apostles, and the method in both cases was to secure the outward act and trust that instruction would follow it. It did not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending with authority to propagate religion; a proselyte as a new convert; baptism as the application of water as a rite of initiation; nominal as existing in name only; and sincerity as freedom from hypocrisy.
webster_full: MISSION, n. A sending or being sent, usually by authority, to perform some service; persons sent to propagate religion.
PROSELYTE, n. A new convert to some religion or religious sect, or to some particular opinion, system or party.
BAPTISM, n. The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church.
NOMINAL, a. Titular; existing in name only; as a nominal distinction or difference is no real difference.
SINCERITY, n. Honesty of mind or intention; freedom from hypocrisy; the quality of being what it appears to be.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: Atlantic kingdom which forcibly baptised its Jewish population in 1497, established the Inquisition in 1536, and carried the Roman mission to four continents.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the mass baptism of the unwilling and the uninstructed, which Portugal practised at home and in part abroad. A rite performed on a man who has not believed does not make him a Christian; it makes him a subject with a false description, and it then exposes him to a tribunal for failing to live up to it. Christ's commission puts teaching in the same sentence as baptism and not after it as an afterthought: go and make disciples, “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19), with the content of the preaching fixed as “repentance and remission of sins” (Luk 24:47).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, and the dictionary states it without diminishing the courage of the men who sailed. Faith is of the heart before it is of the mouth, “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness” (Rom 10:10), and a religion secured by decree earns the sentence Christ quoted against the scribes: “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). The dictionary honours the distances the Portuguese crossed and denies that distance is the measure of a mission. The measure is whether a man was taught enough to believe, and in Lisbon in 1497 nobody was taught anything at all.

pos: n. (the principality of the crown of Aragon, whose Barcelona press printed early vernacular Scripture and whose liberties were broken in 1714)
etymology: From medieval Latin Catalaunia, of disputed origin, perhaps from the castellans of the Frankish march.
biblical_def: Catalonia is the north-eastern principality of the Spanish crowns, with its own language, its own law and, until 1714, its own institutions: the Corts, the Generalitat and the constitutions which the king swore to observe. Barcelona was an early printing centre, and a Catalan Bible was among the earliest vernacular Scriptures printed anywhere in Europe, the Valencian Bible of 1478, which the Inquisition suppressed so thoroughly that only a single leaf survives. Catalonia revolted in 1640 and again took the losing side in the war of the Spanish Succession, after which Philip the Fifth abolished its constitutions in 1714 and its universities, and prohibited official use of the language. The dictionary records Catalonia for the lost Bible. One printed leaf is all that remains of a vernacular Scripture that existed before Luther was born, which is the most compact evidence available that the desire for the Bible in the people's tongue was not a Protestant novelty but a Christian instinct that Rome had to work hard to suppress.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vernacular as native to a country; to suppress as to put down or conceal; a leaf as a part of a book; a constitution as the established form of government; and translation as rendering into another language.
webster_full: VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
SUPPRESS, v.t. To crush; to subdue; to destroy; to conceal; to keep in; to restrain from utterance or vent.
LEAF, n. A part of a book containing two pages; the thin, extended part of a plant.
CONSTITUTION, n. The established form of government in a state; the fundamental rules and principles by which a nation is governed.
TRANSLATION, n. The act of turning into another language; that which is produced by turning into another language.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
corruption_summary: North-eastern Spanish principality whose 1478 Valencian Bible survives in a single leaf, and whose constitutions were abolished in 1714.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the suppression of vernacular Scripture, and Catalonia supplies the hardest piece of evidence for it, because the suppression was so complete that almost nothing is left to argue over. A Bible existed in the people's language in 1478 and was destroyed by a church that claimed to be its guardian. The reason given was the danger of private reading, and the Scriptures answer it with a commendation of exactly that practice: the Bereans “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The text is designed to be understood by the unlearned, which is the whole argument for translation: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). God binds the effect of his word to his own sending and not to an authorisation, so that it “shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11), and Jeremiah describes its force in terms no censor can domesticate: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29). A single surviving leaf is a fragment of a hammer.

pos: n. (the Pyrenean kingdom divided in 1512, whose northern remnant under the Albrets became a Reformed principality and gave France her first Protestant king)
etymology: From Basque nabar, perhaps brown or ploughland, through Spanish Navarra.
biblical_def: Navarre straddled the Pyrenees until Ferdinand annexed the southern and larger part to Castile in 1512, leaving the small northern kingdom of Lower Navarre and Bearn to the house of Albret. That remnant matters out of all proportion to its size. Henri d'Albret married Marguerite of Angouleme, sister of Francis the First, who sheltered French evangelicals including Lefevre d'Etaples and Clement Marot at Nerac; their daughter Jeanne d'Albret established the Reformed religion in Bearn by law in 1560, had the New Testament translated into Basque, and founded the Protestant academy at Orthez; and Jeanne's son Henri became Henry the Fourth of France, abjured in 1593 to gain Paris, and issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. The dictionary records Navarre as the place where the French Reformation was given a state. It also records the end honestly: the dynasty that sheltered the gospel produced the king who traded it for a capital, and his grandson revoked the edict.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a principality as the territory of a prince; abjuration as the renouncing upon oath; an edict as a public ordinance; a refuge as shelter from danger; and apostasy as a departure from one's faith.
webster_full: PRINCIPALITY, n. Sovereignty; supreme power; a prince's territory or jurisdiction; the country which gives title to a prince.
ABJURATION, n. A renunciation upon oath; the act of abjuring or renouncing a former allegiance or opinion.
EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order or ordinance by authority.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.
APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith.
scriptures: For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?
Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;
Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
corruption_summary: Pyrenean kingdom divided in 1512, whose northern remnant became a Reformed principality under Jeanne d'Albret and produced Henry the Fourth of France.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the exchange of a confession for a position, and the dictionary names it in a man it otherwise respects. Henry of Navarre was brave, able and, by the standards of his century, merciful; he was also raised in the Reformed faith by a mother who had risked her small state for it, and he abjured it in 1593 because Paris would not have a Protestant king. Christ asks the question that no political success answers: “For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mat 16:26).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that a choice of this kind is always available in the other direction. Moses is commended for making it, “Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season” (Heb 11:25). The Lord's word to a small body with no prospects is addressed to exactly the position Bearn occupied, “Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luk 12:32). And the word to a church that has fallen remains open as long as there is time for it: “Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works” (Rev 2:5).

pos: n. (the southern Spanish region whose Seville congregation was destroyed in the autos of 1559 and 1560, the one organised Protestant church Spain produced)
etymology: From Arabic al-Andalus, the Muslim name for the peninsula, itself of disputed origin.
biblical_def: Andalusia is the southern region of Spain, Muslim until the thirteenth century and in Granada until 1492, afterwards the richest part of Castile and the gateway to the Indies through Seville. Its claim on this dictionary is a church. In the fifteen-fifties a Protestant congregation formed at Seville around the monastery of San Isidoro del Campo, whose prior and a dozen monks fled in 1557; among them were Casiodoro de Reina and Cipriano de Valera, who abroad produced the Spanish Bible that still carries their names. Those who stayed were arrested from 1557. The autos of 1559, 1560 and 1562 at Seville and Valladolid destroyed the congregation: Constantino Ponce de la Fuente died in prison, Juan Gil and others were burned, and the organised Spanish Reformation ended within five years of beginning. The dictionary records Andalusia because the Reina-Valera Bible, read by millions in Spanish ever since, came out of a church that was killed. What the Inquisition suppressed in one province it could not keep out of a language.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an auto-da-fe is not in Webster, but an act of faith would be a solemn judicial act; a congregation as an assembly met for worship; a version as a translation; a martyr as one who suffers death for his religion; and a legacy as something left by will.
webster_full: CONGREGATION, n. An assembly of persons met for the worship of God and for religious instruction; a collection or assemblage.
VERSION, n. A translation; the act of translating; the rendering of a work from one language into another.
MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the christian faith, or in defense of any cause which he believes to be just.
LEGACY, n. A bequest; a particular thing or certain sum of money given by last will or testament.
SUPPRESSION, n. The act of putting an end to or crushing; concealment; the act of keeping back or restraining.
scriptures: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
corruption_summary: Southern Spanish region whose Seville congregation was destroyed in the autos of 1559 to 1562, and from whose exiles came the Reina-Valera Spanish Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the claim, still occasionally made, that Spain simply never wanted the Reformation. Andalusia answers it with a congregation, a prior, a monastery that emptied, a translation and a list of the burned. The Spanish Reformation existed; it was destroyed by a tribunal within five years, and its survivors spent their exile giving the Spanish language its Bible. John describes that company's victory in terms that do not depend on surviving: “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that a destroyed church can leave a standing legacy. Paul writes from prison about the one thing in the room that is not in custody, “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9), and Luke makes a scattering the means of an advance rather than the end of one: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). God's own guarantee is attached to the sending of his word and not to the safety of the senders, so that it “shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). Every Spanish-speaking believer who reads Reina-Valera is reading what Seville paid for.

pos: n. (the eastern Spanish kingdom of the 1478 printed Bible and of the Morisco population expelled in 1609)
etymology: From Latin Valentia, a Roman colony, from valens, strong.
biblical_def: Valencia was a kingdom of the crown of Aragon, Muslim until 1238 and afterwards holding the largest Morisco population in Spain, descendants of Muslims baptised by compulsion from 1525 who continued their old practice in private. The first printed Bible in a Romance vernacular appeared here, the Valencian Bible of 1478, translated by Bonifaci Ferrer and suppressed almost immediately; a single leaf survives. Valencia was also the city of Juan Luis Vives, the humanist who wrote on the relief of the poor and on the education of women and corresponded with Erasmus and More. In 1609 Philip the Third expelled the Moriscos, some hundred and twenty thousand of them from this kingdom alone, breaking its agriculture for a generation. The dictionary records Valencia as the fullest case of what forced conversion produces: a population counted as Christian, taught almost nothing, policed for a century, and finally deported for being what the policy had made it. The entry stands as a permanent argument against compelling the sacraments.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expulsion as the act of driving out; a convert as one turned from error to truth; hypocrisy as a feigning to be what one is not; relief as the removal of pain or want; and humanity as the kind feelings of man toward man.
webster_full: EXPULSION, n. The act of driving out or away; the state of being driven out; banishment.
CONVERT, n. A person who is converted from one opinion or practice to another; one who renounces error and embraces the truth.
HYPOCRISY, n. Simulation; a feigning to be what one is not; the assuming of a false appearance of virtue or religion.
RELIEF, n. The removal, in whole or in part, of any evil, pain, grief or distress; the alleviation of want.
HUMANITY, n. The peculiar nature of man; the kind feelings, dispositions and sympathies of man toward man.
scriptures: For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: Eastern Spanish kingdom of the suppressed 1478 printed Bible and of the Morisco population forcibly baptised from 1525 and expelled in 1609.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is compelled conversion followed by punishment for its failure, which Valencia carried out over eighty-four years with complete consistency. Muslims were baptised by decree, given no teaching, watched by the Inquisition for keeping their fathers' customs, and finally deported in their tens of thousands. Isaiah's description of religion that reaches the lips and no further is the honest account of what the policy produced: “with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me” (Isa 29:13).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Faith begins inwardly and cannot be legislated, “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness” (Rom 10:10), and a religion imposed by statute is precisely what Christ condemned under the name of men's commandments, “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). The dictionary notes that the better instinct was also present in this city, in Vives's book on the relief of the poor, and that James makes such care a mark of real religion rather than an alternative to it: “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jas 1:27). Valencia had the humanist and the tribunal, and the tribunal set the policy.

pos: n. (the south-eastern Spanish kingdom whose converso population was tried in the great Murcian trials of the fifteen-sixties)
etymology: From Latin Murtia or Arabic Mursiyah, the city founded in 825, of disputed derivation.
biblical_def: Murcia is the dry south-eastern region of Spain between Andalusia and Valencia, a Muslim emirate until the thirteenth century and then a frontier province of Castile with a large converso population in its capital and at Lorca. Between 1560 and 1568 the tribunal of Murcia conducted one of the largest sweeps of the Spanish Inquisition's history against those conversos, with hundreds of prosecutions on evidence that modern historians have shown to have been substantially fabricated by a notary and his associates; the scandal was eventually investigated and the inquisitor and his staff were disciplined, but the sentences had been carried out. The dictionary records Murcia as the clearest proof that a secret tribunal corrupts its own evidence. Where the accused never sees the witnesses, the witnesses can be invented, and the only correction available is the discovery of the fraud long afterwards by the same institution that profited from it. Scripture requires open witnesses for exactly this reason, and had done so for three thousand years before Murcia.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a witness as one who gives testimony; perjury as the wilful swearing of a falsehood; evidence as that which makes clear; a trial as a judicial examination; and justice as the giving to every man his due.
webster_full: WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof; one who sees or knows a fact.
PERJURY, n. The act or crime of wilfully making a false oath, when lawfully administered; false swearing.
EVIDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; proof arising from our own perceptions or from the testimony of others.
TRIAL, n. A judicial examination of the facts in a cause; the examination of the matter in issue before a competent tribunal.
JUSTICE, n. The virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due; equity; agreeableness to right.
scriptures: One witness shall not rise up against a man for any iniquity, or for any sin, in any sin that he sinneth: at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
And the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness, and hath testified falsely against his brother;
corruption_summary: South-eastern Spanish kingdom whose tribunal conducted mass converso trials in the fifteen-sixties on evidence later shown to have been substantially fabricated.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the secret tribunal, and the dictionary names it as a system that produces false testimony by design rather than by accident. At Murcia the accused did not know who had informed on them, so informers could be manufactured; hundreds were condemned and the fraud was uncovered only years later. The law of Moses had already closed that door with a rule about numbers and openness: “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deu 19:15).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is that an accusation must be tested and the accuser exposed to the same risk as the accused. The law requires an inquest into the witness himself, “And the judges shall make diligent inquisition” (Deu 19:18), and the ninth commandment governs the whole matter in six words: “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16). Solomon states the plainest procedural rule in Scripture, and it is the one Murcia abolished: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17). A court that hides the neighbour has given up on justice whatever its verdicts say.

pos: n. (the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, surrendered in 1492 on terms of religious liberty which were broken within ten years)
etymology: From Spanish Granada, the Arabic Gharnatah, of disputed origin.
biblical_def: Granada was the last Muslim state in the peninsula, surrendered by Boabdil on the second of January 1492 under capitulations that guaranteed its people their religion, their mosques, their law, their property and their language. Within seven years Cisneros was conducting mass baptisms and burning Arabic books at Granada; the resulting revolt of 1499 was suppressed and used as the pretext to declare the capitulations void, and in 1502 the Muslims of Castile were ordered to be baptised or leave. The Morisco population that resulted rose again in the Alpujarras in 1568 and was crushed and dispersed across Castile, and the remnant was expelled from Spain after 1609. The dictionary records Granada because it is the plainest instance in European history of a Christian power breaking a sworn treaty for religious ends. The capitulations were not a concession wrung from weakness; they were the terms on which the city opened its gates. An oath sworn to an unbeliever binds exactly as an oath sworn to a brother, and Scripture says so without qualification.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines capitulation as the act of surrendering on stipulated terms; an oath as a solemn affirmation with an appeal to God; a treaty as an agreement between nations; perfidy as the violation of faith; and toleration as the allowance of religious opinions.
webster_full: CAPITULATION, n. The act of capitulating or surrendering to an enemy upon stipulated terms; the treaty or instrument containing the conditions of surrender.
OATH, n. A solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.
TREATY, n. An agreement, league or contract between two or more nations or sovereigns, formally signed by commissioners.
PERFIDY, n. The act of violating faith, a promise, vow or allegiance; treachery; the violation of trust reposed.
TOLERATION, n. The allowance of that which is not wholly approved; allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.
scriptures: Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
Jos 9:19
But all the princes said unto all the congregation, We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them.
Num 30:2
If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
corruption_summary: Last Muslim kingdom in Spain, surrendered in 1492 on guaranteed terms of religion and property which were declared void by 1502.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the treating of an oath as binding only among the orthodox, which is how the capitulations of Granada were set aside. Scripture gives the opposite rule and gives it twice over. The man who may dwell in God's hill is described as one who “sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” (Psa 15:4), and Israel kept a treaty obtained from her by the deceit of the Gibeonites, on the express ground that it had been sworn: “We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them” (Jos 9:19).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. A vow is not a tactic, and the law makes no exception for a change of policy: “he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth” (Num 30:2). Christ reduces Christian speech to a standard that leaves no room for the mental reservations by which the Granada terms were voided, “But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Mat 5:37). The dictionary adds that the Moriscos were never taught; they were baptised, policed and finally deported. A church that breaks faith with the people it has promised is not in a position to catechise them.

pos: n. (the primatial see of Spain, seat of the Visigothic councils and of the 1547 statute of purity of blood)
etymology: From Latin Toletum, a Carpetani town, of pre-Roman origin.
biblical_def: Toledo is the primatial see of Spain and was its political capital until Philip the Second moved to Madrid. Its councils are among the most important assemblies in Western church history: eighteen of them between 400 and 702, which fixed the Visigothic church's discipline, legislated repeatedly and harshly against the Jews, and at the third council in 589 received the conversion of King Reccared from Arianism, with the Nicene creed recited and, by the usual account, the word filioque added to it in the West. In 1547 Archbishop Juan Martinez Siliceo imposed on the cathedral chapter a statute of limpieza de sangre, purity of blood, excluding from office any man with Jewish or Muslim ancestry however orthodox his faith, and the model spread through Spanish institutions. The dictionary records Toledo for that statute above all. It is the point at which a church abandoned the gospel's own account of who may hold office, and substituted descent, and it did so three decades after the Reformation began.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a primate as the chief ecclesiastic; a council as an ecclesiastical assembly; lineage as descent in a line from a progenitor; a creed as a summary of belief; and partiality as an undue bias toward one party.
webster_full: PRIMATE, n. The chief ecclesiastic in the church; an archbishop who has jurisdiction over other bishops.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of ecclesiastics convened for the regulation of the affairs of the church or the determination of doctrine.
LINEAGE, n. Race; progeny; descendants in a line from a common progenitor.
CREED, n. A brief summary of the articles of christian faith; a symbol; that which is believed.
PARTIALITY, n. Inclination to favor one party or one side of a question more than the other; an undue bias of mind.
scriptures: Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:
Jas 2:9
But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.
Eph 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
corruption_summary: Primatial see of Spain, seat of the Visigothic councils and of the 1547 statute of purity of blood which excluded men of Jewish or Muslim descent from office.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the statute of purity of blood, and the dictionary names it as a denial of the gospel rather than a social prejudice with religious trimmings. The whole point of the converso question was that these men had been baptised and professed the Christian faith; the statute said that was not enough, because of their grandfathers. Paul had settled it in one sentence that abolishes exactly this distinction inside the church: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:28).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Peter states the discovery that broke the first barrier of this kind, “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Act 10:34), and James makes partiality in the assembly a transgression of law and not a lapse of manners: “But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors” (Jas 2:9). Paul describes what Christ actually did to the oldest division of all, “who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us” (Eph 2:14). A cathedral chapter that rebuilt that wall in 1547 had other problems than abuses.
